summary:
Selangor is a state of Malaysia and stands under the Malaysian national framework. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature", covering oral and anal sex, with up to twenty years' imprisonment plus whipping, regardless of the gender of the participants, whether the act is consensual, or whether it takes place in private. Section 377D adds an undefined "gross indecency" offence carrying up to two years. The Human Dignity Trust country profile, last updated 16 December 2025, records that these provisions have been enforced in recent years, apply to both men and women, are usable against transgender people, and are not confined to Malaysian citizens, so they reach foreign visitors in Selangor. Non-Muslim visitors fall under the federal Penal Code alone.

Selangor maintains a state Sharia layer above the federal code. The Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 criminalises cross-dressing and a man posing as a woman, alongside liwat and musahaqah, with penalties reaching three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These offences bind Muslims only, and enforcement rests with the Selangor Islamic Religious Department. Because the enactment contains no definition of transgender dress, the boundary between acceptable and offending presentation is set by officers on the ground.

Enforcement in Selangor is active and documented. A Selangor Sharia court sentenced five men to six or seven months' imprisonment with six strokes of the cane. At least 1,733 people had attended state "rehabilitation programmes" as of June 2021, under a crackdown on LGBT people running since the 2018 general election; Human Rights Watch and Justice For Sisters found that such programmes internalise discrimination and foment self-hatred among those ordered into them.

The case of Nur Sajat shows how far Selangor authorities will go to enforce gender norms. She is a transgender woman and cosmetics entrepreneur who in 2021 failed to appear in a Selangor court to answer criminal charges for "insulting Islam" brought on the basis of her attire. The state religious department issued a warrant for her arrest, announced that it had mobilised 122 religious-affairs officers to hunt her down, and later sought her extradition from Thailand. She was permitted to remain under UNHCR protection and has since settled in Australia.

Violence against transgender women in the state is lethal. A trans woman was killed in Klang, Selangor, in June 2019, the third such killing of a trans woman in Malaysia in fewer than two months, and killings of this kind have gone unpunished.

The Federal Court struck down provisions of the Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 in 2021 as exceeding the power of the state legislature. The ruling turned on which legislature may enact the offence rather than on the substance of the prohibition, and nothing under the federal Penal Code was decriminalised; cross-dressing and same-sex conduct remain chargeable in Selangor through the federal sections and the surviving state provisions.

The national framework also governs entry, relationships and remedies. There is no explicit visa rule for transgender visitors; the closest documented statement of entry policy is a 2001 declaration by then-Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad that Malaysia would deport any visiting foreign cabinet minister or diplomat who is gay. Same-sex marriage and any form of partner recognition are unavailable, and Malaysian law provides no protection against discrimination or hate crimes on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation.
tangentialFactors:
Selangor is one data point in a nationwide pattern. Human Rights Watch and Justice For Sisters covered Kuala Lumpur, Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Kelantan, Penang, Pahang and Kedah in their 2022 documentation of state-backed discrimination, and every one of Malaysia's thirteen states plus the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya maintains Sharia enactments criminalising cross-dressing or same-sex conduct.

Other states show the same machinery under different labels. The Federal Court struck down sixteen Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024, again on federalism grounds, and Terengganu's 2022 amendment extended court-ordered counselling or religious rehabilitation to a year. Enforcement against social venues has also escalated nationally: a Kuala Lumpur gay bar raid in August 2018, a Halloween party with LGBTQ participants in 2022, eleven shopping malls raided in May 2023 over the sale of Pride watches, and the arrest of 208 men under section 377B at a Chow Kit sauna on 28 November 2025.

Arbitrary arrest, strip-searches and sexual assault by religious officials during detention have been documented against transgender people across Malaysia over decades, including a mass arrest of sixteen trans women at a wedding in June 2014 and repeated arrests of individual women more than twenty times.
localsOnly:
Selangor's Islamic Religious Department enforces the state Sharia enactments against residents, and the absence of any statutory definition of transgender dress means presentation is judged by officers rather than by a legal standard. The 1,733 recorded attendees of state rehabilitation programmes as of June 2021 were ordered into them through this enforcement apparatus.

Sharia courts in Malaysia may commit women convicted of musahaqah to an approved home for up to six months and may order cross-dressing and other offenders into counselling or rehabilitation in a religious institution for up to six months in some states. Local LGBT communities also face pressure through the 1982 National Fatwa Committee edict that sex is determined at birth and unaffected by reassignment surgery; the edict was never gazetted and is not legally binding, but it is applied in practice, including to invalidate marriages involving transgender people.

Gender-marker changes on identity cards are refused in practice. The Registration Department rejected such applications until August 2016, when the Kuala Lumpur High Court ordered it to update a trans man's identity card on the basis that Article 5(1) of the Federal Constitution guarantees a right to live with dignity in one's gender; that judgment was overturned on appeal in 2017. The only successful documented marker change is historical, dating to 1975.

Residents have no statutory recourse: Malaysian law provides no protection against discrimination or hate crimes on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation, and no political party pursues LGBTQ legal reform.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether the arrest warrant issued for Nur Sajat in Selangor in 2021 remains live, and whether the deployment of 122 religious-affairs officers continues after her departure from Malaysia. Her current status in Australia does not settle the status of the Selangor proceedings.

Unresolved: the current on-the-ground frequency of Selangor enforcement. The sources date the rehabilitation figure to June 2021 and the sentencing and warrant events to 2021-2022; no post-2022 Selangor enforcement data is sourced here, and the general profile last-updated date of 16 December 2025 speaks to the national provisions rather than to state enforcement volume.

Unresolved: which specific provisions of the Syariah Criminal Offences Enactment 1995 survived the Federal Court's 2021 ruling and which were voided, and whether the state legislature has since re-enacted replacement offences. The inventory establishes that the judgment rested on state legislative power, not on the substance of the prohibition.

Not sourced here: any recorded case of a foreign transgender visitor being charged under Selangor's state Sharia provisions rather than the federal Penal Code, and any Selangor-specific guidance on documentation or screening at entry.
